c.tagline: City of dreaming spires, centuries of scholarship, and cobbled college quads

taxi.fareNote: Licensed black cabs can be hailed on the street or found at ranks; minicabs are cheaper but must be pre-booked by phone or app

emergency.note: Dial 999 for emergencies (police, ambulance, fire); call 111 for non-urgent medical advice via the NHS

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Bike theft is rife, and Cornmarket Street and the station area see occasional pickpocketing and phone snatching.

hood_desc: Home to the historic university colleges, the Bodleian Library, and Radcliffe Camera. Pedestrianized streets and the Covered Market make it easy to explore on foot, though it gets crowded with tourists and students alike.
A charming Victorian-era neighborhood of terraced houses along the Oxford Canal, known for indie cafes, the Phoenix Picturehouse cinema, and a bohemian, arty feel.
A diverse, lively area southeast of the centre with some of Oxford's best curry houses, live music venues, and student-friendly bars along Cowley Road.
An affluent residential suburb north of the centre with boutique shops, delis, and a village-like high street popular with families.
A hillside suburb east of the centre, home to the John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford Brookes University, and the famous fibreglass Headington Shark sculpture.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink everywhere.

transit.hours: Roughly 5:30am-midnight, reduced service late night and Sundays
transit.pay: Contactless card, mobile app, or cash on board
transit.note: Oxford has no metro or tram; buses, walking, and cycling are the main ways to get around, along with Park & Ride from the edge of the city

train: Direct trains to London Paddington (~1 hour)
Direct trains to Birmingham, Reading, and Manchester
bus: Oxford Tube and National Express 24-hour coach services to London

tip.r: Restaurants often add a 10-12.5% service charge; if not included, 10% is appreciated. Not customary for taxis or pubs beyond rounding up

food.name: Oxford sausage
food.desc: A skinless herbed sausage of pork, veal and lemon zest dating to the 18th century, usually served with mash and onion gravy in a college pub.

places.name: M. Feller Son and Daughter
places.note: Organic butcher in the 1774 market, the traditional source for Oxford sausages.

places.name: The Turf Tavern
places.area: Bath Place, hidden off Holywell Street
places.note: 13th-century alley pub reached by lanes; classic sausage and mash by the fire.

places.name: The Bear Inn
places.note: Oxford's oldest pub, from 1242, tiny rooms lined with cut-off college ties.

food.name: Pub pie and mash
food.desc: Short-crust or puff-topped pies of steak and ale, chicken and leek or game, served with mash, peas and a jug of gravy.

places.name: Pieminister
places.note: Small market cafe doing pies with mash, peas and gravy for under 10 pounds.

places.name: The White Horse
places.note: Narrow one-room pub squeezed between bookshops; a Morse filming favourite.

places.name: Lamb and Flag
places.note: Historic pub owned by St John's College, reopened and back doing proper pub food.

food.name: Oxford Blue cheese
food.desc: A creamy, tangy blue made in Oxfordshire since 1995 in the Stilton tradition but softer, with notes of white wine and chocolate on the finish.

places.name: Oxford Cheese Company
places.note: Independent cheesemonger that sells Oxford Blue and its own Oxford Isis.

places.name: The Old Parsonage
places.note: Serves blue-cheese scones on its afternoon tea in a 1660 stone hotel.

places.name: Alpha Bar
places.note: Long-running salad and sandwich counter that puts local cheeses to work.

food.name: Cream tea and scones
food.desc: Warm scones with clotted cream and jam beside a pot of tea; in Oxford it is usually taken in a college-adjacent tearoom or a grand hotel drawing room.

places.name: The Grand Cafe
places.note: On the site of England's first coffee house from 1650; ornate gilded room.

places.name: The Randolph Hotel
places.note: Victorian-Gothic hotel drawing room for the full afternoon tea treatment.

places.name: Vaults and Garden Cafe
places.note: Vaulted 1320s congregation house with a garden facing the Radcliffe Camera.

food.name: Sunday roast
food.desc: Roast beef with Yorkshire pudding, roast potatoes and gravy, eaten slowly in a riverside pub; the fixed weekly ritual of Oxfordshire pub life.

places.name: The Perch
places.note: Thatched 17th-century pub across Port Meadow, reached on foot along the river.

places.name: The Trout Inn
places.note: Riverside inn beside a weir, familiar from Inspector Morse; book for Sundays.

places.name: The Rickety Press
places.note: Neighbourhood Jericho pub with a well-regarded roast and local ales.

food.name: Oxford marmalade breakfast
food.desc: Dark, chunky Seville-orange marmalade first made in an Oxford shop in 1874, piled on toast as part of a full English or a college-style breakfast.

places.name: The Grand Cafe
places.note: Traditional breakfasts with marmalade and toast in a mirrored belle-epoque room.

places.name: Vaults and Garden Cafe
places.note: Organic, locally sourced breakfasts under medieval vaults.

places.name: Oxford Covered Market cafes
places.note: Several counters do a full English with marmalade and preserves sold nearby.

food.name: Real ale in a historic pub
food.desc: Cask ales from Oxfordshire brewers such as Hook Norton and Brakspear, hand-pulled in pubs that have served students and dons for centuries.

places.name: The Turf Tavern
places.note: Ancient beer garden pub famous for its rotating cask list and its alumni.

places.name: The Bear Inn
places.note: Oxford's oldest pub; low beams, tie collection and well-kept ale.

places.name: The Kings Arms
places.note: Wadworth-run corner pub that has been pouring since 1607.

food.name: Pimm's by the river
food.desc: Gin-based Pimm's No. 1 with lemonade, cucumber, mint and fruit, drunk in a punt or on a river terrace through the Oxford summer.

places.name: Cherwell Boathouse
places.note: Hire a punt then drink Pimm's on the riverside terrace where they are moored.

places.name: The Head of the River
places.note: Wide Thames-side terrace beside the punt station, packed on sunny days.

places.name: The Perch
places.note: Big meadow garden by the Thames, a classic summer Pimm's stop.

landmarks: Radcliffe Camera
England's earliest circular library, a Palladian 1749 masterpiece rising from cobbled Radcliffe Square, the single most photographed silhouette in Oxford's dreaming spires.
Bodleian Library
One of Europe's oldest libraries, whose Divinity School's fan-vaulted ceiling and Duke Humfrey's medieval reading room have starred in the Harry Potter films.
Christ Church College
Oxford's grandest college, founded by Cardinal Wolsey, combining Tom Tower, a cathedral, and the Tudor dining hall that inspired Hogwarts' Great Hall.
Bridge of Sighs (Hertford Bridge)
An ornate 1914 skyway linking two quadrangles of Hertford College over New College Lane, affectionately nicknamed for its Venetian lookalike.
Ashmolean Museum
Britain's oldest public museum, a neoclassical treasure-house spanning Egyptian mummies, Raphael drawings and Guy Fawkes' lantern, all with free admission.
Magdalen College
C.S. Lewis's college of honey-hued cloisters, a Great Tower serenading May Morning crowds, and a riverside deer park grazed since the 1700s.
University Church of St Mary the Virgin
The medieval church at Oxford's ceremonial heart, whose 13th-century tower rewards a narrow spiral climb with the definitive view over Radcliffe Square.
Sheldonian Theatre
Christopher Wren's first major building, a Roman-inspired ceremonial hall of 1669 where students still matriculate and graduate beneath a painted allegorical ceiling.
Pitt Rivers Museum
A gloriously atmospheric anthropology collection behind the Natural History Museum, its dim Victorian cases crammed with shrunken heads, totem poles and amulets.
Oxford Covered Market
A historic 1774 market beneath timber roofs, where traditional butchers and cobblers trade alongside cookie shops, florists and the famous Ben's Cookies stall.

train.note: No international trains - Eurostar runs from London St Pancras. GWR reaches London Paddington in about an hour from Oxford station, with CrossCountry services north to Birmingham and beyond and the newer Oxford Parkway station on the Chiltern line to London Marylebone. Advance fares open 12 weeks out.

bus.note: No direct international coaches. The Oxford Tube (https://www.oxfordtube.com/) and Airline coaches to London Victoria, Heathrow and Gatwick run around the clock, often every 15 minutes, and are cheaper than the train though slower - many people prefer them for airport runs. Long-distance National Express services use Gloucester Green.

ferry.note: Oxford is inland with no passenger ferry. Punts and narrowboats on the Cherwell and the Thames are for hire by the hour rather than scheduled transport.

half.name: Blenheim Palace
half.blurb: Winston Churchill's birthplace, a Baroque palace with landscaped grounds in Woodstock, is about twenty minutes from Oxford.

half.name: Burford
half.blurb: A honey-stone Cotswolds market town on the River Windrush lies roughly forty minutes west of Oxford.

half.name: Bath
half.blurb: Roman baths and Georgian crescents sit about ninety minutes southwest of Oxford.

half.name: Stratford-upon-Avon
half.blurb: William Shakespeare's birthplace and its riverside theater district are roughly an hour from Oxford.
